entries.title: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart: 2026 year-to-date in review
entries.summary: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart onboarded over 100 new models from 30 providers in the first three quarters of 2026. This recap covers the model-onboarding highlights and JumpStart enhancements, including the simplified Model Hub, pre-configured deployment options, and Hugging Face deep link integration.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Amazon SageMaker JumpStart: 2026 year-to-date in review

Amazon SageMaker JumpStart is a machine learning (ML) hub within Amazon SageMaker AI that provides access to a curated catalog of AI models, solution templates, and example notebooks. It reduces the time it takes to go from model selection to deployment. You can use it to evaluate open source large language models (LLMs), deploy a vision model for document understanding, or fine-tune a compact model on your own data.

SageMaker JumpStart serves three primary use cases:

  • Model discovery and evaluation — Browse hundreds of foundation models (FMs) from providers like Alibaba (Qwen), NVIDIA, Google, Mistral, Cohere, IBM, and more. Each model card includes architecture details, benchmarks, licensing information, and sample notebooks.
  • One-click deployment — Deploy your choice of model to a SageMaker real-time inference endpoint with pre-configured settings optimized for your workload (low cost, low latency, throughput, or balanced). No manual container or instance configuration required.
  • Model customization — Fine-tune models directly from the console or SDK using techniques like low-rank adaptation (LoRA), supervised fine-tuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Serverless customization options reduce infrastructure management.

You can access SageMaker JumpStart through the SageMaker Studio console (Models → JumpStart models), programmatically through the SageMaker Python SDK, or directly from Hugging Face using the recently launched deep link integration.

2026 onboarding at a glance

From January through September 2026, SageMaker JumpStart onboarded over 100 new models across 30 distinct providers. This represents a significant expansion of the catalog, driven by the accelerating pace of open source model releases and growing customer demand for choice across model architectures, sizes, and capabilities.

Here’s a breakdown of the leading contributors and a link to our SageMaker JumpStart page:

  • Alibaba (Qwen): 29 models spanning reasoning (Qwen 3.8-27B), large-scale mixture-of-experts (Qwen3.5-122B-A10B), agentic workflows (Qwen-AgentWorld-35B-A3B), code generation (Qwen3-Coder-Next, Qwen 3 Coder 30B), speech recognition (Qwen3-ASR-1.7B), text-to-speech (Qwen3-TTS), embeddings (Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B), and reranking (Qwen3-Reranker-4B).
  • NVIDIA: 17 models including the Cosmos3 world foundation model family (Super, Edge, Nano), Cosmos Reason 7B, MSA-Search, Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, Nemotron-3-Super-120B (FP8 and BF16), Nemotron3 Ultra, Nemotron-Nano-12B-v2, Nemotron 3 Nano Omni (multimodal), and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for vision-language.
  • Mistral: 7 models including the Ministral-3 family (3B, 8B, 14B in standard and BF16) and Voxtral-Mini-4B-Realtime for speech.
  • Google: 6 Gemma 4 variants, including gemma-4-31B-it, E2B-it, E4B-it, 26B-A4B-it, assistant, and NVFP4 quantized.
  • IBM: 4 models including Granite 4.0 h-micro/small/tiny and granite-speech-4.1-2b for multilingual automatic speech recognition (ASR) across 6 languages.
  • Cohere: 4 models including Command A (A100) and Rerank v3.5, v4.0 Fast, and v4.0 Pro for retrieval augmentation.
  • Others: 33 models from MiniMax, Zhipu AI (GLM), DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Allen AI, Microsoft, Meta (Muse Spark), Reflection (Beam), Black Forest Labs, JetBrains, OpenBMB, BharatGenAI, Kakao, OpenFold, and more.

Model onboarding highlights

The models onboarded in 2026 reflect several focused priorities in how we expand the SageMaker JumpStart catalog. These aren’t only industry trends. They represent the areas where we see strong customer demand and significant opportunity to help customers build production AI applications on SageMaker.

Expanding the NVIDIA open-model portfolio

NVIDIA is one of our significant model providers, and in 2026 their contribution extended well beyond language models. The Cosmos3 world foundation models, available in Super, Edge, and Nano tiers, bring video generation, physics simulation, and action planning into a single architecture for physical AI applications such as robotics, autonomous systems, and digital twins. Combined with Nemotron models spanning from efficient edge inference (Nano-12B) to large-scale reasoning (Super-120B), SageMaker JumpStart now offers a broad portfolio of NVIDIA open models. If you build on NVIDIA hardware, you can deploy these models on SageMaker with optimized containers and pre-configured endpoints.

Closing the multimodal gap

Customer workloads increasingly require models that process more than text. In 2026, we prioritized onboarding models that handle vision, speech, and document understanding natively. NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano Omni processes text, vision, and speech in a single model. Google Gemma 4 adds vision-language capabilities across multiple sizes. IBM granite-speech-4.1-2b handles speech recognition and translation across six languages. Mistral Voxtral-Mini supports real-time speech understanding. These additions mean customers can avoid chaining separate preprocessing models for multimodal workloads.

Making creative AI accessible

Image and video generation moved from niche to mainstream in 2026. We onboarded FLUX.2 Small Decoder and FLUX.2-klein-base-4B from Black Forest Labs for fast text-to-image generation, Meta Muse-Glimmer-30B for multimodal agentic workflows, and NVIDIA Cosmos3 for video generation. With these models, you can access creative AI capabilities with the same one-click deployment experience you use for language models.

Prioritizing efficient and quantized models

Not every workload requires a frontier-scale model, and many customers are focused on optimizing inference costs as they move to production. We onboarded multiple quantized and compact models: Zhipu AI GLM-5.2 FP8 delivers strong performance with a reduced memory footprint. JetBrains Mellum2-12B uses a mixture-of-experts architecture with only 2.5B active parameters for code generation. OpenBMB MiniCPM5-1B packs multimodal capabilities into 1 billion parameters. Microsoft Phi-4-mini-instruct and IBM Granite 4.0 h-tiny demonstrate that compact models serve production workloads on instance types like ml.g5.xlarge. These models can optimize latency and total cost of ownership (TCO) for targeted use cases.

Onboarding purpose-built models for targeted tasks

General-purpose LLMs are versatile, but purpose-built models are optimized for specific tasks. In 2026, we onboarded Qwen-AgentWorld-35B-A3B for autonomous AI workflows with native tool-calling. GLM-OCR, LightOnOCR, and DeepSeek-OCR handle document text extraction. Qwen3-Reranker-4B and Cohere Rerank v4.0 improve retrieval precision in Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines. langcache-embed-v3-small provides lightweight embedding for semantic search. Qwen3-ASR and Qwen3-TTS bring speech recognition and synthesis. OpenFold3 supports protein structure prediction for scientific computing. With these models, you can build pipelines where each stage uses the specialized tool for the job, rather than forcing a single model to do everything.

Broadening provider diversity

Reducing concentration risk in model selection is important for enterprise customers. In 2026, we expanded the catalog to include 30 providers, up from a more concentrated set in prior years. Alibaba Qwen is the single largest contributor with 29 models spanning reasoning, coding, speech, and retrieval. Zhipu AI and DeepSeek add competitive LLMs and specialized OCR. MiniMax and Moonshot AI contribute emerging architectures. Cohere brings reliable reranking. BharatGenAI and Kakao expand regional model coverage. This breadth gives customers more options for performance, cost, licensing, and language support.

SageMaker JumpStart enhancements in 2026

Beyond model onboarding, SageMaker JumpStart also shipped significant improvements in 2026 that reduce friction across the model lifecycle, from discovery to deployment.

Simplified Model Hub on the SageMaker AI console

Previously, discovering SageMaker JumpStart models required navigating into SageMaker Studio and finding the SageMaker JumpStart section in the left navigation. The new Model Hub experience surfaces the full SageMaker JumpStart catalog directly on the SageMaker AI console landing page. You can browse models by category and filter by input/output modality, publisher, model size, license, and framework. You can also view sample notebooks and open models inside Studio with a single click. This avoids the multi-step navigation that slowed initial exploration.

Pre-configured endpoint deployment options

Choosing the right instance type, serving container, and optimization settings for a model deployment typically required manual benchmarking across dozens of combinations. SageMaker JumpStart now offers named deployment configurations, with optimization options for:

  • Balanced — An even tradeoff between cost, latency, and throughput for general-purpose workloads.
  • Throughput optimized — Maximum tokens per second using techniques like Speculative Decoding, ideal for high-volume batch processing.
  • Latency optimized — Lowest Time to First Token (TTFT), prioritizing speed for interactive applications.
  • Cost optimized — Lowest infrastructure cost per request, suitable for workloads that can accept higher latency.

These configurations include Neuron-optimized setups for AWS Inferentia and AWS Trainium instances, reducing deployment complexity and infrastructure costs. You can deploy a model with a single click and the right optimization profile, rather than spending weeks benchmarking configurations manually.

Hugging Face deep link integration

A new integration with Hugging Face connects model discovery directly to SageMaker Studio, for onboarded models. When browsing models on Hugging Face, you can choose Deploy on SageMaker AI or Customize and Deploy on SageMaker AI. You land directly in a configured Studio environment with the model pre-loaded, permissions pre-configured, and GPU quota visibility built in. This avoids the need to set up AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles, create a domain, or configure permissions before experimenting.

Getting started

There are three ways to get started with SageMaker JumpStart:

  • SageMaker Studio console — Open SageMaker Studio, navigate to Models → JumpStart models, and browse the catalog. Choose a model to view its details, then choose Deploy or Customize.
  • SageMaker Python SDK — Deploy models programmatically using the SageMaker Python SDK. Visit the SageMaker JumpStart model catalog for SDK examples and deployment guides.
  • Hugging Face deep link — Browse the HuggingFace Model Hub and choose Deploy on SageMaker AI to land directly in Studio for SageMaker JumpStart onboarded models.

Each model on SageMaker JumpStart includes deployment configurations, sample notebooks, and documentation. For a hands-on walkthrough, see our related blog post on “Deploy and evaluate models with Amazon SageMaker JumpStart”.

Conclusion

The first three quarters of 2026 have been a period of significant progress for Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. With over 100 new models onboarded from 30 providers, the catalog now spans a wide range of capabilities. These include frontier reasoning models, multimodal vision-language models, creative AI for image and video generation, speech recognition and synthesis, optical character recognition (OCR) and document understanding, embedding and retrieval models for RAG, agentic workflow models, and specialized scientific computing models.

These onboarding priorities reflect where we see the strongest customer demand and the greatest opportunity to accelerate AI adoption on AWS. They include expanding the portfolio, closing the multimodal gap, making creative AI accessible, prioritizing efficiency and quantization, onboarding purpose-built models, and broadening provider diversity.

Combined with the enhancements like simplified Model Hub, pre-configured deployment options, and the Hugging Face deep link integration, SageMaker JumpStart continues to lower the barrier between model discovery and production deployment. Visit the SageMaker JumpStart model catalog to explore the full lineup.

Next steps

There are many ways to get started with SageMaker JumpStart. Try one of these out for yourself!

  • Evaluate models and choose the right one for you
  • Learn how to Deploy from HuggingFace to SageMaker Studio
  • Use pretrained models in case-based deployments
  • Design a Physical AI model factory on SageMaker HyperPod

entries.title: Pegasus 1.5 from TwelveLabs is now available in Amazon Bedrock
entries.summary: TwelveLabs Pegasus 1.5 is now available in Amazon Bedrock. The video language model turns long-form video into structured, timestamped metadata: define the moments that matter and get every matching segment back as JSON, with new video segmentation, multimodal prompting with reference images, and on-the-fly processing of up to two hours of video.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Pegasus 1.5 from TwelveLabs is now available in Amazon Bedrock

On Oct 9, 2026 we announced the availability of TwelveLabs’ Pegasus 1.5 on Amazon Bedrock. Pegasus 1.5 is a video language model that turns long-form video into structured, timestamped metadata. You describe the moments that matter to your workflow, and the model returns every matching segment as JSON.

Video represents a significant and complex category of unstructured data, yet most of it remains unsearchable and underutilized. Extracting structured, actionable insights from that content has historically required labor-intensive manual review or fragmented toolchains.

With earlier versions of Pegasus, you can point the model at a clip, ask a question, and get an answer. Now, Pegasus 1.5 analyzes the entire video, finds every segment that matches user-defined criteria, and returns structured, timestamped metadata. It also introduces video segmentation, multimodal prompting with reference images, and on-the-fly processing.

With Pegasus 1.5 on Amazon Bedrock, you can analyze videos directly from an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) URI or a base64 string with no pre-indexing required, and your data remains within the AWS data boundary.

In this post, we cover what’s new in Pegasus 1.5, how the model is packaged on Amazon Bedrock, and how to send your first request. We then walk through video segmentation, structured JSON output, and multimodal prompting.

What’s new in Pegasus 1.5

Pegasus 1.5 has the following changes compared to previous versions:

  • Time-based metadata generation. You define the segments, events, or domain-specific cues that matter to your workflow, such as editorial segments, sports plays, speaker changes, or brand appearances. Pegasus 1.5 returns every matching segment as JSON, with start and end times and the requested fields populated.
  • Multimodal prompting. A segment definition can combine a text description with a visual reference. This makes it possible to locate a specific product, logo, or person, along with what they are doing on screen.
  • On-the-fly processing. No ingestion pipeline or pre-indexing step is required. Videos are sent directly from Amazon S3 and results are returned in the response.
  • Extended processing capacity. Pegasus 1.5 analyzes videos up to two hours long in a single request, up from one hour in Pegasus 1.2.

Pegasus 1.5 retains and enhances the core capabilities that made Pegasus 1.2 a powerful tool for video understanding, including:

  • Video-to-text generation: Creates detailed textual descriptions based on video content.
  • Granular visual comprehension: Analyzes objects, on-screen text, and numerical content within video frames.
  • Temporal grounding: Accurately identifies timestamps of specific events within videos.
  • Multimodal understanding: Combines visual, audio, and textual information for comprehensive analysis.
  • Multilingual support: Full support for English, with partial support for Arabic, Chinese, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, Thai, and Vietnamese.

Multimodal prompting: Adding visual context to your queries

Pegasus 1.5 introduces multimodal prompting, so you can include reference images alongside your text prompts. This is useful when you want to ask the model about specific objects, people, or scenes that are easier to show than describe.

For example, you can provide a product image and ask the model to identify every moment where that product appears in a video. Or you can provide a reference image of a specific logo and ask the model to detect brand appearances and their timestamps. This capability enhances the precision of video analysis, and opens up use cases such as visual brand monitoring, product placement analysis, and image-guided content search.

Use cases

Pegasus 1.5 is designed for organizations that manage large volumes of long-form video:

  • News and broadcast archives: Teams can define editorial segments, topics, and speaker changes once, then catalog years of footage that was previously searchable only by transcript keywords.
  • Sports broadcasters and leagues: Detect plays, scoring events, and other key moments across full-length game footage, speeding up highlight production.
  • Streaming applications: Scene-level metadata supports moment-based recommendations, contextual ad placement, and segment-level brand safety review.

In each case, people remain part of the workflow. Their work shifts from finding and tagging every moment by hand to reviewing and refining the metadata generated by the model.

Input requirements

Pegasus 1.5 supports the following video specifications:

  • Duration: Up to 2 hours.
  • File size: Up to 2 GB from Amazon S3, or up to 25 MB as a base64 string.
  • Resolution: 360×360 to 5184×2160.
  • Aspect ratio: Between 1:1 and 2.4:1, or their inverses.
  • Formats: FFmpeg-supported formats.

Now available

TwelveLabs Pegasus 1.5 is available today on Amazon Bedrock in the US West (Oregon) AWS Region. Check the full Region list for future updates, and visit the Amazon Bedrock pricing page for pricing information. Pegasus 1.5 is billed through AWS Marketplace, so its charges appear on your AWS bill and in AWS Cost Explorer under TwelveLabs rather than Amazon Bedrock.

To get started:

  • Visit the TwelveLabs models page on Amazon Bedrock to learn more about the model family.
  • Review the Pegasus 1.5 model card for feature support, Region availability, and sample code.
  • Send us feedback at AWS re:Post for Amazon Bedrock or through your usual AWS Support contacts.

We’re excited to see what you build with TwelveLabs Pegasus 1.5 in Amazon Bedrock.

entries.title: How Deepgram optimized voice AI at scale with AWS Trainium
entries.summary: Deepgram worked with the AWS Forward Deployed Engineering team to port its Nova-3 speech-to-text model to AWS Trainium2 for offline batch inference. This post covers porting to the AWS Neuron stack, kernel-level tuning, a data-parallel Rust runtime, and the throughput and cost results on batch transcription.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

How Deepgram optimized voice AI at scale with AWS Trainium

As voice becomes a first-class modality for AI, Deepgram’s models span speech-to-text, text-to-speech, and voice agents. They now process quadrillions of audio tokens a year for more than 200,000 developers and 1,400 organizations. Customers use them through the Deepgram API or run them in their own environments, including on Amazon SageMaker AI.

For Deepgram, serving efficiency determines how much audio the system can process for a given infrastructure budget. High-volume batch workloads put heavy pressure on that budget, so the more efficiently each accelerator hour is used, the more audio Deepgram can serve on the same fleet. That made inference efficiency a natural target and Deepgram turned to AWS AI chips to improve it. They worked with AWS to bring its Nova-3 speech-to-text model to AWS Trainium2 for offline batch workloads such as contact-center analytics and medical transcription.

The engagement began with Deepgram delivering Nova-3 as standard PyTorch code. Over several months, Deepgram and the AWS Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE) team ported Nova-3 to AWS Trainium2 in PyTorch reconstruction and tuned it for the new hardware. The final configuration runs eight model replicas on a single Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) trn2.3xlarge instance. On Deepgram’s offline, throughput-oriented batch workloads, that setup processed 11–70 percent more audio per dollar than the compute options Deepgram had been running. We measured this using instance pricing at the time of the evaluation. These gains help Deepgram scale efficiently, keep shipping better models, and bring them to customers at lower prices. These benefits can extend to customers who self-host Deepgram models in their own virtual private cloud (VPC) on Amazon SageMaker AI. There, Deepgram and AWS continue to improve ease of setup, reliability, and observability.

In this post, we walk through the full inference optimization effort on Trainium: porting Nova-3 to the AWS Neuron software stack, the kernel-level tuning that followed, the data-parallel Rust runtime that lets Deepgram’s own model server call Trainium, and the throughput and cost results we measured on batch transcription.

Optimizing Nova-3 to Trainium2 with native PyTorch

Starting with standard PyTorch code, we used TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch integration of the Neuron Compiler, which supports both eager execution and 

torch.compile
. We ran Nova-3 in eager mode on Trainium2 first and checked which operations fell back to the CPU, then compiled with 
torch.compile
. The compiled path ran every model operation on Trainium2 with no CPU fallbacks detected.

We compiled the encoder and decoder as separate static-shape graphs using 

torch.compile
. Throughout, we checked numerical accuracy at two levels: layer-level output consistency against CPU, and the end-to-end Word Error Rate (WER), which had to stay in line with Deepgram’s reference values and target.

From that working baseline, we kicked off the optimization work by replacing several layers with fused kernels from the public NKI Library (NKILib), a collection of pre-built reference kernels written with the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI). The kernels covered operations such as fused QKV projections, fused feed-forward network (FFN) layers, and depthwise 1D convolution.

We optimized for throughput and, by extension, cost efficiency, targeting Deepgram’s offline inference workloads. Throughput is reported as a relative gain over a baseline configuration rather than as absolute audio processed per second, and we swept batch sizes 1–128 to find the throughput-maximizing batch size.

Kernel-level tuning with Neuron Explorer and NAD

Enabling kernels is only the first step of an optimization flywheel: enable an NKI kernel (custom or from NKILib), profile the workload, then either tune the existing kernel or replace it with a new one based on the profiling insights. This cycle repeats until the performance target is met. At each step, a different part of the Neuron stack accelerates the work: NKILib provides drop-in replacement kernels, Neuron Explorer is the go-to tool for profiling Neuron workloads, and the Neuron Agentic Development (NAD) toolkit speeds up profiling analysis and kernel tuning through its profiling and kernel-writing skills.

In our case, the NKILib kernels got us most of the way, and profiling showed where a hand-written kernel would do better. Each time, the NAD profiling skills took us from a Neuron Explorer profile to a root cause, and the NAD kernel-writing skills helped produce the replacement kernels.

LayerWhat we found and changedGain
FFNThe reference kernel’s tiling schedule reloaded the full set of projection weights from off-chip memory for every token tile, so memory bandwidth limited throughput as the token count grew. Our hand-tuned kernel loads each weight tile once, reuses it across multiple token tiles, and pipelines weight reads with on-chip compute.2.0x lower latency compared to the reference kernel at batch size 96
Depthwise conv1dThe experimental NKILib kernel framed the operation as an implicit general matrix multiply (GEMM), which left Tensor Engine utilization low. We rewrote it as a broadcast multiply-accumulate loop on the Vector Engine, reaching full engine utilization, enough to more than offset the Vector Engine’s lower peak throughput.1.5x speedup compared to the reference kernel at batch size 96
Conv2dThe model’s conv2d layers hit a compilation bottleneck: beyond batch size 32, these layers prevented the model from compiling as a single graph. Since NKILib had no conv2d kernel, we wrote one from scratch in NKI. The kernel went through several profiler-informed iterations following the flywheel described earlier, unlocking batch sizes above 32.Up to 50x on the convolution module at batch sizes ≤32

Data-parallel runtime in Rust

Each Trainium2 device features eight physical NeuronCores, exposed by default as four logical NeuronCores (LNC2). Because each Nova-3 model instance fits comfortably on a single physical core, we reduced the number of physical cores per logical core to one (LNC1). This configuration lets us host eight model replicas (DP8) per Trainium2 device. Inputs are processed concurrently while maximizing per-device throughput. The data-parallel runtime is driven by a work-stealing queue with one thread per replica.

Deepgram’s production serving stack is written in Rust, so porting Nova-3 to Trainium2 required more than compiling the model: it also had to run without Python or PyTorch in the serving path. We therefore built a lightweight runtime in which Rust coordinates model replicas through a shared work-stealing queue. A C layer loads and executes ahead-of-time-compiled Neuron Executable File Format (NEFFs) directly through the Neuron Runtime API (

libnrt
). The runtime integrates directly with Deepgram’s serving architecture and reproduced the reference token sequences exactly at every tested batch size.

We benchmarked it against multithreaded (MT) and multiprocessing (MP) Python data-parallel runtimes. Compared with the MP baseline, the Rust runtime removes the overhead of the Python interpreter entirely. Compared with the MT baseline, it further alleviates global interpreter lock (GIL) serialization, so dispatch calls from concurrent worker threads are no longer contended within a single process. These gains matter because Nova-3 performs a sequence of small decoder calls for each audio chunk, making host-side dispatch the bottleneck at low batch sizes. The throughput improvement is therefore largest there, and remains meaningful even at the throughput-maximizing batch size. There, the Rust runtime delivered a 7.5% throughput gain over the multiprocessing Python baseline.

Cost saving impact

We measured price-performance as audio processed per dollar. On Deepgram’s offline, throughput-oriented batch workloads, the single-device Trainium2 setup (trn2.3xlarge) processed 11–70 percent more audio per dollar than the compute options Deepgram had been running.

Conclusion

In this post, we demonstrated how Deepgram and the AWS FDE ported the Nova-3 speech-to-text PyTorch model to Trainium hardware using TorchNeuron, which provides native PyTorch framework integration for AWS Trainium. We improved performance by replacing layers directly with pre-built kernels from NKILib. We then assessed performance using Neuron Explorer and used the Neuron Agentic Development (NAD) profiling skills to query profiling data and accelerate performance troubleshooting. Building on these insights, we adapted kernel source code using the NAD kernel-writing skills. Finally, we built a lightweight Rust data-parallel runtime for AWS Trainium, calling the Neuron Runtime API from Rust. Our setup demonstrated cost savings in offline, throughput-oriented scenarios, validating AWS Trainium as a viable and efficient option for Deepgram’s inference workloads.

To try this approach on your own models, start with the AWS Neuron documentation, which covers the compiler, the runtime, and the supported frameworks. The Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) guide explains how to write the kernels described in this post, and the NKI samples repository holds the reference kernels we started from. The Neuron developer tools documentation covers the profiling and agentic tooling we used here, including Neuron Explorer and Neuron Agentic Development. For instance sizes and pricing, see Amazon EC2 Trn2 Instances. For help scoping a similar port, contact the AWS Forward Deployed Engineering.

entries.title: Push-based KV transfer to improve TTFT and TPOT for disaggregated inference in vLLM
entries.summary: vLLM's prefill-decode disaggregation splits LLM inference across engine instances but must transfer the KV cache between them. This post introduces a push-based NIXL connector that moves transfer coordination off the critical path, delivering up to 3x better TTFT and 30% better TPOT in benchmarks on Amazon EC2 P5en instances with AWS EFA.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Push-based KV transfer to improve TTFT and TPOT for disaggregated inference in vLLM

vLLM is an open-source inference and serving engine for large language models (LLMs). LLM inference has two distinct phases: prefill, which processes the input prompt and builds the key-value (KV) cache, and decode, which uses that cache to generate output one token at a time. These phases have different compute, memory, and scaling characteristics. Prefill-decode (P-D) disaggregation runs them on separate engine instances, allowing each phase to scale and be optimized independently. This can improve resource utilization, throughput, and latency under load. However, it also requires transferring the KV cache from the prefill instance to the decode instance before token generation can begin, making efficient KV transfer critical to time-to-first-token (TTFT).

One of the ways vLLM performs this transfer is through the NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library (NIXL) connector, which moves KV blocks over interconnects that support Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA), such as AWS Elastic Fabric Adapter (AWS EFA, the low-latency RDMA network used across servers in AWS). On supported instance types, AWS EFA supports GPUDirect RDMA and Neuron Direct RDMA. NIXL can therefore transfer KV blocks directly between GPU or AWS Trainium device memory without staging through host memory. The default mode for NIXL connector is pull-based: After the prefill instance finishes computing the prompt KV cache, the router relays the source metadata, including the prefill block IDs, to the decode instance. The decode instance then allocates destination blocks, prepares the NIXL transfer, and initiates NIXL READ to pull the KV blocks from the prefill instance. Because these coordination and setup steps occur sequentially after prefill and before decoding can begin, they extend the TTFT critical path, as shown in the following timeline.

This post introduces a push-based NIXL connector that moves post-prefill transfer coordination and setup off the critical path. If you run disaggregated prefill/decode inference with vLLM, push mode can improve application responsiveness by reducing TTFT and TPOT, particularly at high request rates.

In our benchmark on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) P5en instances connected with EFA, push mode delivered up to 3x better TTFT and up to 30 percent better time-per-output-token (TPOT) compared to pull mode (see the Performance data section) for the Qwen3-32B model. Results depend on workload and configuration.

We built and validated the feature on AWS Trainium instance clusters connected with EFA, and then we contributed it to vLLM as an accelerator-agnostic feature. The results here are from an Amazon EC2 P5en (GPU) cluster with EFA, showing the gains carry over to GPUs. This post explains the push-based architecture, transfer flow, threading model, performance results, and how to reproduce the benchmark.

Push-based KV transfer

This section explains the push-based design: its architecture, the transfer protocol, and the threading model that keeps KV transfer off the critical path.

Architecture overview

Push-based transfer improves TTFT and decode throughput for two reasons:

  • It removes the serialization of the pull model by overlapping producer and consumer work. The decode instance registers its target blocks in advance while the producer is still computing KV. The transfer then begins as soon as the producer’s blocks are ready, rather than after a consumer-side ID-discovery round trip, removing that round trip from the path to first token.
  • It moves the transfer-setup time off the decode instance. That setup runs on the prefill side and on a background thread. It prepares the NIXL descriptors and submits the transfer, so the decode instance does not spend those cycles during its latency-critical token-generation phase.

The net effect is lower TTFT and higher output-token throughput on the decode instance.

The push connector coordinates three actors: the decode instance registers its target blocks up front, the prefill instance matches each request and issues the transfer, and a dedicated background thread carries the KV write off the engine’s forward-pass loop. The following diagram shows how these pieces fit together.

Implementation details

The protocol has three logical steps.

1. Registration (decode side). When the decode instance allocates local blocks for a request requiring remote prefilling, it prepares a registration describing where the prefill instance should write the KV: its own identity and the block locations it has just reserved. Within the same engine step, the worker transmits this registration to the prefill instance as a NIXL notification. Because registration happens at allocation time, the connector knows the destination blocks before the prefill instance completes prefill.

2. Rendezvous (prefill side). The registration from the decoder and the completion of prefill on the producer can arrive in either order, and the connector handles both. If the registration arrives first, the producer holds it until its own prefill finishes. If prefill finishes first, the producer holds the request’s blocks until the registration arrives. Whichever event happens second triggers the transfer. The connector pairs requests by ID, and the matching accounts for reissued requests, correctly associating preempted or retried requests.

3. Transfer (prefill side). Once a request is matched, the producer establishes a connection to the decode instance (if one does not already exist) and issues an NIXL WRITE that copies the KV blocks directly into the decoder’s registered memory, addressing each destination tensor-parallel rank. The producer and consumer may use different internal block layouts. Each side maps block locations to its own physical layout at transfer time, allowing different block sizes on each side. Each WRITE carries a completion notification that NIXL delivers to the decode instance once the data arrives. The decoder counts these notifications, one per producer rank that writes into it. It treats the KV as received only after all expected notifications have arrived, at which point the request proceeds to decode.

Threading model

The push connector separates model execution from KV-transfer preparation by using a dedicated background transfer thread on each prefill worker. At the start of a request, the decode main loop allocates its destination KV blocks and registers them with the prefill instance while the prefill main loop computes the prompt KV cache. After both the destination registration and prompt KV are ready, the prefill main loop hands the KV blocks to the background thread and quickly returns to model execution.

The background thread establishes or reuses the NIXL connection, maps the request’s KV block IDs to memory descriptors, merges contiguous blocks into larger transfer regions, and submits the NIXL WRITE to the decode instance. When NIXL completes the transfer, it sends a completion notification to the decode instance, which then begins token generation. Keeping descriptor preparation and transfer submission off the latency-critical main loops prevents this per-request work from delaying model execution. The following diagram shows these main-loop and background-thread handoffs for a single request.

Timing comparison of pull and push

The following diagram summarizes the pull and push transfer flows described in the preceding sections and highlights their effect on TTFT. Although both modes use the same NIXL and EFA/RDMA data path, pull performs the metadata relay and decode-side setup after prefill, while push overlaps decode-side setup with prefill. As a result, push removes these operations from the post-prefill critical path, allowing decoding to begin sooner.

The two modes also involve a routing tradeoff. Pull mode allows the router to select a decode instance after prefill completes, which provides greater flexibility for load-aware routing and quality-of-service management. Push mode selects the decode instance earlier so that destination setup can overlap with prefill. In return, under comparable load, the prefill instance can release its KV blocks sooner because the transfer starts as soon as both the prompt KV and destination registration are ready.

Performance data

For evaluation, we used Qwen3-32B model on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with EFA. To isolate P→D transfer performance, we configured the benchmark to disable prefix caching with 

--no-enable-prefix-caching
. This configuration makes the decode node retrieve the full KV cache from the prefill node for every request. Otherwise, overlapping prompts could reuse the decode node’s local cache and bypass the transfer, which would produce misleading comparison results.

The following chart compares TTFT for push and pull KV transfer. We sweep input lengths 1k–16k and request rates of 1–8 queries per second (QPS). At low load and short prompts, the two modes perform almost identically. As QPS and input length grow, pull mode degrades sharply, reaching about 1,744 ms at 8 QPS and 16k. Push mode stays far lower at roughly 540 ms, around 3x reduction. The gap opens because pull mode posts NIXL descriptors inline on the decode worker, synchronously within its engine loop, so that work stalls token generation. Push mode moves it to a background thread, off the critical path.

This chart shows TPOT under the same conditions. The pattern mirrors TTFT. At light load, push and pull are close, around 5.6–5.8 ms. As load and input length rise, pull climbs to about 10.4 ms at 4–8 QPS and 16k, while push holds near 7 ms. The reason is that push offloads descriptor preparation and transfer submission from the decode worker. Token generation is not starved, so per-token latency stays flat even at high concurrency and long contexts.

How to run benchmark

To reproduce our 1P1D benchmark configuration, one prefill node and one decode node, using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with EFA, refer to the detailed instructions in the Reproducing our results guide. The guide covers environment setup, launching the vLLM prefill and decode servers, running the benchmark, and collecting results. The feature can run on other supported configurations, but performance results will vary depending on the hardware, model, workload, and network configuration.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed how the push-based KV connector overlaps prefill computation with decode-side block allocation and registration, removing the post-prefill router round trip and decode-side transfer setup from the critical path. This reduces TTFT and TPOT, particularly at high request rates. In our Qwen3-32B benchmark on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with EFA, push mode provided up to a 3x improvement in TTFT and 30 percent improvement in TPOT compared with pull mode. Results vary by workload and configuration. To use push mode, configure both the prefill and decode servers to use 

NixlPushConnector
instead of 
NixlConnector
.

Choose the push-based connector when early decode node selection is acceptable and lower TTFT is the priority. The pull-based connector remains the better fit for workloads that require bidirectional KV transfer or defer decode-instance selection until after prefill for load-aware routing. vLLM supports both push- and pull-based KV connectors, so you can select the approach that best fits your deployment.

As a future improvement, we are exploring bringing the background NIXL threading model to the pull-mode connector, moving NIXL setup off the critical path so that pull-mode workloads could benefit from the same optimizations. We have opened a pull request to explore this.

Related resources

Acknowledgments

We thank the vLLM community for their support in maintaining this feature.

entries.title: Improve TTFT for multi-turn agentic workloads with bi-directional KV transfer in vLLM
entries.summary: Multi-turn agentic workloads reprocess growing conversation context each turn, driving up latency. See how bi-directional KV cache transfer lets prefill and decode nodes reuse previously computed context across turns, cutting time to first token by up to 1.6x for Qwen3-32B and 3.3x for GLM-5-FP8 on Amazon EC2 P5en instances with EFA.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Improve TTFT for multi-turn agentic workloads with bi-directional KV transfer in vLLM

Multi-turn agentic workloads build on accumulated context as an agent reasons, invokes tools, and incorporates earlier results. With each new turn, the client resends the conversation history, including system instructions, prior prompts, tool results, and model responses, causing the growing context to be processed repeatedly. In Prefill-decode (P-D) disaggregation, each request is split across specialized nodes: the prefill node processes the prompt and builds its key-value (KV) cache, then the decode node retrieves those KV blocks and generates the response.

Conventional disaggregated serving, however, only transfers KV cache in one direction: from prefill to decode node. This one-directional flow creates two inefficiencies for multi-turn workloads. First, after generating a response, the decode node holds KV cache entries for both the prompt and the newly generated tokens. When processing the next turn, the prefill node cannot retrieve those entries, so it must recompute the KV projections for the previous response tokens. Second, the decode node maintains the session state while the prefill nodes don’t, increasing the probability of cache eviction for active sessions on the prefill nodes. On a full cache miss, the prefill node must recompute KV projections for the entire conversation history, including system instructions, prior user requests, tool results, and model-generated responses. As the conversation grows, this redundant work consumes more accelerator capacity and increases time to first token (TTFT).

When you build conversational assistants and agentic applications, longer interaction histories can increase latency and consume accelerator capacity through repeated prefill computation. In this post, we show how bi-directional KV cache transfer lets prefill and decode nodes reuse previously computed context across turns, which improves accelerator utilization and helps applications sustain responsive TTFT as conversations grow.

In our multi-turn benchmarks on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) P5en instances, bi-directional KV transfer reduced TTFT by up to 1.6x for Qwen3-32B and up to 3.3x for zai-org/GLM-5-FP8 (see the Performance data section). Results vary with workload and configuration. The instances are connected with AWS Elastic Fabric Adapter (AWS EFA), a low-latency remote direct memory access (RDMA) network used across servers in AWS. On supported instance types, AWS EFA supports GPUDirect RDMA and Neuron Direct RDMA to move KV blocks directly between GPU or AWS Trainium device memory on the prefill and decode nodes.

We originally built and validated the feature on AWS Trainium instance clusters connected with EFA and contributed it to vLLM as an accelerator-agnostic capability. The results presented here are from an Amazon EC2 P5en GPU cluster with EFA, showing that the benefits also carry over to GPUs. This post explains the bi-directional KV transfer architecture, router metadata flow, KV-block retention and recompute controls, performance results, and how to reproduce the benchmark.

Bi-directional KV transfer

Bi-directional KV transfer is a mechanism in which a decode node returns previously computed KV to a prefill node on subsequent turns of a conversation. This avoids recomputing shared context on the prefill node and is governed by a configurable KV recompute threshold. It mitigates both computational-redundancy scenarios described earlier. To make it work, the KV must survive past the turn that produced it and travel in the reverse direction, coordinated by a KV-cache-aware router.

NIXL KV connector enhancements for bi-directional transfer

We extended the NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library (NIXL) KV connector to let prefill nodes consume remote KV blocks, similar to how decode nodes already consume KV blocks that the prefill node provides. This is not a trivial change, because the two node types are architecturally different: prefill nodes compute KV representations for new prompt tokens and can provide complete prompt KV blocks. Decode nodes lack the capability (or efficiency) to generate complete KV representations and can only serve previously cached KV blocks. As a result, prefill and decode nodes still carry their own roles and logic for computing the metadata of remote and local KV blocks. The actual KV transfer mechanism (a NIXL READ), however, is common to both the 

P->D
and 
D->P
directions.

The following diagram first shows the existing flow in blue. The router sends the request to prefill node, prefill node computes the prompt KV and returns its block metadata, and the router forwards the request and metadata to decode node for the standard P→D NIXL READ. The numbered red path illustrates the bi-directional KV transfer additions: (1) decode node retains eligible KV blocks after generation, (2) returns their metadata in the streaming response, and (3) the router caches that metadata for the next prefill request. Prefill node then (4) checks the remotely reusable KV after it applies local cache matches, (5) queues an asynchronous receive when the reusable token count meets the threshold, and (6) performs a D→P NIXL READ before computing the remaining suffix.

KV-cache-aware router

vLLM includes connector-side support for bi-directional KV transfer, while coordinating KV reuse across conversation turns requires a KV-cache-aware router. vLLM GitHub provides an example proxy that implements the flow used in this post which can be adapted for your environment.

The KV-cache-aware router is a lightweight, stateful control-plane component between the client, prefill, and decode nodes. It maintains an in-memory mapping from the client-provided 

conversation_id
to decode’s 
kv_transfer_params
. The router stores only block-location metadata, not KV tensors, and obtains that metadata from the response stream rather than separately querying decode node.

The following diagram shows how the router manages KV metadata across conversation turns. On the first turn, the cache lookup misses and the request follows the standard P→D flow. The router then saves decode’s metadata from the response stream. On later turns, the router retrieves that metadata using the 

conversation_id
so prefill can reuse KV from decode. It then refreshes the metadata after generation for the next turn.

Block retention TTL

Normally a decode instance frees a request’s blocks as soon as generation finishes. Under bi-directional KV transfer mode, it holds them for a configurable lifetime (

decoder_kv_blocks_ttl
, default 480 seconds) and publishes their location and expiry. The conversation’s KV, both prompt prefix and generated response, then stays available for the next turn. For a turn that arrives before the time to live (TTL) expires, prefill node reuses the KV. One that arrives later falls back to normal prefill. Because this TTL is fixed and not renewed, tune it to the expected time between turns to balance KV reuse against accelerator-memory usage. A natural next improvement is to extend the heartbeat-renewed lease to the decode side. A decode instance could then reclaim blocks as soon as a conversation goes idle rather than at the end of a fixed timer.

KV recompute threshold

KV reuse isn’t always faster than local recomputation. For a short reusable prefix, interconnect and coordination overhead can exceed the time needed to recompute the tokens. The 

kv_recompute_threshold
setting, which defaults to 64 tokens, controls this decision. Prefill node recomputes when the token count to compute is below the threshold and pulls KV from decode node when it is at or above the threshold. Deployments can tune this value based on model computation time, KV size, and interconnect performance.

Performance data

For evaluation, we used Qwen3-32B and GLM-5-FP8 models on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with EFA. To emulate scenarios in which the prefill node has evicted its local cache or the router selects a different prefill node that does not have the conversation’s KV blocks, we disabled prefix caching on prefill node with 

--no-enable-prefix-caching
.

Across both the models, turning on bi-directional KV transfer reduces prefill computation on multi-turn conversations, and the benefit typically grows with prompt length. With the feature OFF, the prefill instance recomputes the entire grown context each turn, so TTFT rises steeply. Qwen3-32B climbs from 158 ms at 2k to 778 ms at 24k, and GLM-5-FP8 from 500 ms at 2k to 2,334 ms at 20k. With it ON, the decode instance’s retained KV is reused instead of recomputed, keeping TTFT far flatter. Qwen3-32B rises only from 122 ms to 460 ms over the same range (about a 1.6x reduction at the longest prompt), while GLM-5-FP8 rises from 358 ms to 702 ms and runs up to 3.3x below the recompute path at long prompts. The prefill-duration breakdown explains why.

Bi-directional transfer adds a small KV-transfer time (about 30 ms to 130 ms for Qwen3-32B; about 29 ms to 110 ms for GLM-5-FP8), but the prefill compute it removes far outweighs that KV-transfer time. As a result, the total prefill duration with transfer ON (Qwen3-32B: 128 ms to 414 ms; GLM-5-FP8: 316 ms to 541 ms) stays well below the recompute-only path (Qwen3-32B: 153 ms to 744 ms; GLM-5-FP8: 500 ms to 2,331 ms). The larger GLM-5-FP8 model shows a bigger absolute and relative gap, since its higher per-token recompute time makes KV reuse pay off even more as models and contexts scale.

Qwen3-32B

The following chart plots TTFT against prompt length for Qwen3-32B, comparing bi-directional KV transfer ON versus OFF.

The next chart breaks the prefill duration for the same runs into its recompute and KV-transfer components.

Together the charts show TTFT staying nearly flat with the feature ON while the OFF path climbs steeply as context grows, because the small KV-transfer time is far outweighed by the recompute it removes.

zai-org/GLM-5-FP8

The same two views follow for GLM-5-FP8. The first plots TTFT against prompt length with the feature ON versus OFF.

The second breaks the prefill duration into its recompute and KV-transfer components.

GLM-5-FP8 shows a much larger gap than Qwen3-32B, up to about 3.3x lower TTFT at long prompts, because its higher per-token recompute time makes KV reuse pay off even more as context length grows.

How to run benchmark

To reproduce our 1P1D benchmark configuration, one prefill node and one decode node, using Amazon EC2 P5en instances with EFA, follow the step-by-step instructions in the Reproducing our results guide. The guide covers environment setup, launching the vLLM prefill and decode servers, running the benchmark, and collecting results. The feature can run on other supported configurations, but performance results will vary depending on the hardware, model, workload, and network configuration.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed how bi-directional KV cache transfer can reduce TTFT as an agent’s conversation history grows. In P-D disaggregated deployments, the feature lets prefill node reuse KV blocks retained by decode node across turns, reducing repeated computation. Configurable block-retention and recompute thresholds determine when reuse occurs. On a 1P1D deployment using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with EFA, at the longest prompt lengths tested, we observed TTFT reductions of 1.6x for Qwen3-32B and 3.3x for zai-org/GLM-5-FP8. Results depend on the workload and deployment configuration. To implement this in your environment, use vLLM v0.21.0 or later with NixlConnector, enable 

bidirectional_kv_xfer
on both prefill and decode servers, use a kv-cache-aware router, and follow the GitHub reproduction guide.
